messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Patel is a 35-year-old tax consultant who came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was “just tired” and that work stress was catching up with him. Before returning to the U.S., he had spent several weeks as a relief worker in a war zone, helping distribute supplies and assisting with evacuations after shelling in a civilian area. The moment that now sits at the center of his distress is fragmented in his telling: he remembers smoke hanging low over a damaged street, people shouting, and moving toward a building where families had been sheltering. He recalls seeing bodies brought out, the air thick with burning and dust, and being forced to choose who could be moved first. A burial area had formed nearby because there was nowhere else to take the dead. What stays with him most is the conviction that others were looking to him and that he did not do enough.

Since returning home, seemingly ordinary moments in his daily life as a tax consultant have become charged with danger. If he passes a cluster of smokers outside his office building, the smell of smoke catches in his throat and his whole body reacts before he can think. If a client raises their voice in irritation, even calmly, he feels himself tense and brace. When a colleague mentioned attending a funeral for her father, he had to leave the break room. These moments do not stay small. The smell, the word funeral, the sight of anger on someone’s face immediately pull up pieces of the war-zone scene, and he can suddenly feel his body folding into the same protective crouch he had taken there, his hands drawn up toward his face as if shielding himself.

The memories come in a disjointed way that unsettles him further. He cannot place what happened in a clear sequence, only broken images and bodily sensations. At night, when the house is quiet, he finds it harder to feel safe than during the day; the dark seems to leave too much room for something to happen. Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming outside, the heating system clicking on—make him jump sharply, and afterwards the half-formed memories push closer. In those moments he is not only remembering smoke and shouted instructions; he is flooded with shame, gripped by the sense that he had been in the position to protect people and failed.

That meaning has spread far beyond the event itself. Arjun has come to believe that the world no longer works according to any dependable rules, that catastrophe can arrive without warning and that decency offers no protection. He feels cut off from other people, including friends who try to welcome him back into normal routines. When triggers hit—a funeral notice online, smoke from a neighbor’s grill, a flash of irritation in someone’s voice—they do not just evoke memory; they confirm what he now believes about himself and the world. He hears in another person’s anger the same helpless urgency of those days overseas, and he reads his own reaction as proof that he is fundamentally different from everyone around him.

Over time he has organized his life around trying not to feel any of this. He avoids the part of the city where a humanitarian fundraiser was held because it reminds him of the field site and the people he could not save. When something upsetting catches him off guard, he covers his face with his hands, a gesture that briefly blocks the room around him but also puts him back into the body posture of the event. He has also begun turning away from invitations that might make him feel good—his wife’s plans for dinners out, celebrations with cousins, even a weekend trip—because hope and pleasure feel almost disloyal. If he lets himself enjoy anything, he fears he is erasing the dead or excusing his failure. These habits have narrowed his life, and in the narrowing he feels even more separate and ashamed.

The strategies that are meant to keep him steady seem instead to tighten everything. Avoiding reminders leaves the memories more confused and jagged, never fully sorted into the past. Covering his face when distressed makes the bodily sense of the event more immediate. Staying away from happy occasions has strained his marriage; his wife experiences him as absent and unreachable, which he silently takes as further evidence that he does not belong with other people anymore. At work, his concentration has worsened during client meetings, especially late in the day or after being startled by a noise in the office, and he has become increasingly vigilant by evening, checking locks and scanning sounds outside the apartment.

What finally brought Arjun in was a recent family funeral. He had agreed to attend for the sake of his parents, but the smell of incense and cremation smoke, the gathered grief, and a relative’s curt voice sent him spiraling into a familiar collapse of body memory, shame, and alarm. He spent much of the service with his face in his hands, then left abruptly and sat in his car shaking. He told his wife afterward that he was afraid he was becoming someone who could no longer live in ordinary life—someone always waiting for the next sign of danger, always one reminder away from that street. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is not to forget what happened, but to be able to remember it without feeling condemned by it.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly show Arjun’s negative appraisals causing him to become more sensitive to or generate triggers/reminders.
The vignette shows threat and alarm occurring alongside shame and beliefs, but it does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not explicitly state that Arjun’s sense of threat increases attention to, sensitivity to, or creation of triggers/reminders.

Although avoidance and other maladaptive strategies are described as narrowing his life, the vignette does not clearly state that these strategies lead to increased exposure to or sensitivity to triggers/reminders.
The vignette describes maladaptive strategies maintaining memories and shame, but it does not explicitly convey that these strategies heighten Arjun’s sense of threat or danger.
